title: A Shepherd Boy Chosen as King
overview: God sends Samuel to secretly anoint young David as Israel's future king, while the rejected King Saul sinks into torment and unknowingly brings David into his own court.

parts.label: A risky secret mission (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: Saul has been rejected as king, and choosing a replacement while he still rules could look like treason, so Samuel fears for his life and is told to go and hold a real sacrifice. The town leaders tremble because a visit from Samuel was rare and might mean trouble, and the people prepare themselves with washing and setting themselves apart so they can share in the sacred meal.

parts.label: Looks are not the measure (vv. 6-10)
parts.note: Samuel is impressed by Jesse's tall eldest son, making the same mistake people made with Saul, who was also chosen partly for his height. God answers that people judge by appearance but God looks at the heart, meaning a person's inner character, and seven sons are passed over.

parts.label: The youngest is anointed (vv. 11-13)
parts.note: David, the youngest, was out with the sheep and not even invited, yet he is the one Samuel anoints by pouring oil on his head to mark him as God's chosen king, and God's Spirit comes on him. The title Messiah means 'anointed one,' and Christians read David's anointing in Bethlehem as pointing ahead to Jesus, born in that same town and from David's family line.

parts.label: Saul's troubled mind (vv. 14-17)
parts.note: As God's Spirit leaves Saul, the text says a harmful spirit from the LORD torments him, reflecting an ancient way of seeing everything, good or painful, as coming from God's hand. Whether this describes a literal spirit or a deep despair and dark moods is genuinely debated, and his servants suggest music from a lyre, a small stringed harp, to calm him.

parts.label: David enters Saul's service (vv. 18-23)
parts.note: David is recommended as a skilled player and capable young man, and Jesse sends gifts of food and wine as a sign of respect to the king. Saul grows fond of David and makes him his armor-bearer, a trusted personal attendant, with no idea that this comforter is the king chosen to replace him.

disagreement: Christians differ on how to understand the 'evil spirit from the LORD,' some reading it as a real spirit God allowed or sent and others as the text's way of describing Saul's mental and emotional collapse.
think: What would change if people were judged by their inner character rather than by how they look or where they rank?
